2	
3	This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.
4	
5	Handheld vacuum lifter with grip-loss alarm
6	
7	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is disclosed. The lifter includes a rigid body with a handle and a suction cup that carries a flexible sealing lip. An electric vacuum pump is disposed within the rigid body and draws air through a port to create a vacuum. A pressure sensor monitors the grip vacuum and drives a warning indicator when vacuum is lost. A rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump. The warning indicator is configured to activate before a load can be dropped.
8	
9	1. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter comprising:
10	    a rigid body comprising a handle;
11	    a suction cup carried by the rigid body, the suction cup comprising a flexible sealing lip;
12	    an electric vacuum pump disposed within the rigid body, the electric vacuum pump configured to draw air through a port to create a vacuum;
13	    a pressure sensor configured to monitor the vacuum;
14	    a warning indicator driven by the pressure sensor, the warning indicator configured to activate when the vacuum is lost; and
15	    a rechargeable battery configured to power the electric vacuum pump.
16	
17	2. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter of claim 1, wherein the warning indicator is configured to activate before a load can be dropped.
18	
19	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter for glass and stone panels is disclosed. The lifter includes a suction cup 10 that carries a flexible sealing lip 12 on a rigid body 14. The rigid body 14 also includes a handle 16. An electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed inside the rigid body 14 and is configured to draw air through a port 22 to create a vacuum. A pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum. The pressure sensor 30 drives a warning indicator 32, which activates when vacuum is lost. The warning indicator 32 is configured to warn a user before a load can be dropped. A rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20.

1	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to move glass panes, stone slabs, and similar flat panels on site by suction gripping. A suction cup is pressed against the face of the panel, air is removed from the space enclosed between the cup and the panel, and the resulting difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in that enclosed space clamps the cup to the panel so that the panel can be carried.
2	
3	A suction grip is only as good as its seal. Dust on the panel, a textured or porous surface, a nick in the sealing lip, a change in temperature, or simply the slow permeation and leakage that occurs over minutes of handling will all bleed air back into the enclosed space. As air returns, the clamping force falls. The failure is progressive and, from the point of view of the person holding the panel, silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes until the cup lets go, at which point a heavy panel is already falling.
4	
5	Vacuum lifting equipment has therefore long been fitted with vacuum monitoring. In one known lifter for transporting loads having an adhesion surface, a suction plate assembly carries projecting annular seals defining a vacuum chamber connected to a main vacuum source, a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that can be started by an emergency switch is additionally provided, and a pressure pickup associated with the vacuum chamber is coupled with a malfunction alarm such that the alarm is turned on when a preset limit pressure is exceeded during vacuum operation [REF:US-5310232-A]. That equipment is a suspended plate assembly with a main vacuum source and a separate emergency vacuum source; the alarm is described as a malfunction alarm tied to a preset limit pressure, and the reference does not describe the limit pressure in terms of the vacuum still needed to keep hold of the load.
6	
7	Control systems for vacuum lift equipment have also been described in which a programmable controller interprets feedback from vacuum level sensors and battery sensors and responsively provides warnings and limits or alters machine functions, including evaluating a change in measured vacuum level over time to determine a rate of vacuum level change that may be caused by a leak and outputting a warning indication when that rate exceeds a threshold rate [REF:US-10518985-B2]. Such a system is built around a controller with memory, stored records, and machine-function interlocks, and its leak warning is a response to how fast the vacuum is changing rather than to where the vacuum sits relative to the point at which the grip would fail.
8	
9	Powered suction devices in a hand-carried format are also known. An electric vacuum suction lifter has been described having a main body with a suction surface carrying first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space, a control unit, a vacuum pump controlled by the control unit to draw air from the sealed space, a pressure sensing unit that measures the pressure of the sealed space to generate instant pressure information, a battery unit that is charged by external power equipment and powers the control unit, pump, and pressure sensing unit, a start button, a pressure relief button, and at least one handle by which a member gripped by the device can be carried [REF:US-10625955-B2]. In that device the instant pressure information is compared with a high predetermined pressure and a low predetermined pressure: reaching the high predetermined pressure stops the pump, and falling below the low predetermined pressure restarts the pump. A warning unit is described as being operated when the detected battery power is below a predetermined battery power, and warning information relating to pressure is described as being transmitted to an external electronic device. A closely similar electric suction cup has likewise been described, in which the pressure detection unit detects the pressure between the suction cup and the component in real time and the vacuum pump automatically acts again when that pressure is lower than a second predetermined pressure [REF:CN-110630621-B].
10	
11	Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1].
12	
13	Two shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and the low pressure value at which it acts is chosen with reference to the working vacuum, not with reference to how much grip is left. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone. Second, where a warning is given, it is given either on a condition unrelated to grip (battery state), on a rate of change, or at a preset limit whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established. None of these guarantees the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.
14	
15	There remains a need for a self-contained, cordless, hand-held vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing at a point on the decay curve at which the grip has not yet failed.
16

Because the warning vacuum level is above the release vacuum level, the grip vacuum on a decaying grip reaches the warning vacuum level first and the release vacuum level only afterwards. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is disclosed. The lifter has a rigid body comprising a handle, and a suction cup carried by the rigid body. The suction cup comprises a flexible sealing lip which, when placed against a workpiece, bounds a sealed region between the suction cup and the workpiece. An electric vacuum pump is disposed within the rigid body and draws air from the sealed region through a port so as to establish a grip vacuum in the sealed region, the grip vacuum holding the suction cup, and hence a load carried by the suction cup, against the workpiece. A pressure sensor monitors the grip vacuum. A warning indicator is carried by the rigid body and is driven by the pressure sensor. A rechargeable battery carried by the rigid body powers the electric vacuum pump.

The grip vacuum is treated throughout this disclosure as a positive magnitude: it is the amount by which the pressure in the sealed region is below the ambient pressure outside the lifter, so that a larger grip vacuum means a firmer grip and a decaying grip is a falling grip vacuum.

The warning indicator activates when the grip vacuum falls to a warning vacuum level. The warning vacuum level is not the level at which the grip fails and is not the level at which the pump is asked to run again. It is a level that is greater than a release vacuum level, the release vacuum level being the grip vacuum below which the suction cup can no longer retain the load. Because the warning vacuum level is above the release vacuum level, the grip vacuum on a decaying grip reaches the warning vacuum level first and the release vacuum level only afterwards. The warning indicator therefore activates while the suction cup is still holding the load, and there is grip in reserve at the moment the user is told. That reserve is what the user spends in getting the panel onto a stand, against a wall, or back onto the stack.

This ordering of levels is what makes the alarm useful in a hand-held tool rather than merely informative. A frame-mounted or suspended lifter can respond to a failing grip by itself, by cutting in a second vacuum source or by refusing to move. A cordless handheld lifter has no such recourse: the only actuator available is the person holding the handle, and a person needs an interval in which to act. Defining the warning threshold with respect to the release vacuum level, rather than with respect to the working vacuum level or with respect to a rate of change, is what makes that interval exist by construction rather than by luck.

In embodiments, the warning indicator remains active for as long as the grip vacuum stays at or below the warning vacuum level, so that a grip which is decaying continuously produces a warning which persists rather than a single transient. In embodiments, the warning indicator is positioned on the rigid body where it is perceptible to a user whose hand is on the handle and whose eyes are on the panel. In embodiments, the pressure sensor is in fluid communication with the sealed region, so that what is monitored is the grip vacuum acting on the workpiece itself rather than a proxy elsewhere in the machine.

Because the electric vacuum pump, the pressure sensor, the warning indicator, and the rechargeable battery are all carried by the rigid body, the lifter grips, monitors, and warns without any hose, cord, or external controller, and can be taken up a ladder or onto a scaffold in one hand.

A method of lifting a workpiece with such a lifter is also disclosed. The method includes placing the flexible sealing lip against the workpiece, drawing air from the sealed region with the electric vacuum pump to establish the grip vacuum, monitoring the grip vacuum with the pressure sensor while the load is carried, and activating the warning indicator when the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level, that is, while the suction cup still retains the load and before the grip vacuum has fallen to the release vacuum level.

7	FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. 11	FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. 36	
37	The electric vacuum pump 20 first raises the grip vacuum to a working vacuum level 62, which is the grip vacuum at which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is fit to lift. 38	
39	Two levels lie below the working vacuum level 62 on the vacuum axis 70. The lower of the two is the release vacuum level 66, at which the suction cup 10 lets go. The elapsed time between the crossing of the warning vacuum level 64 and the arrival of the grip vacuum trace 60 at the release vacuum level 66 is the warning interval 68.
40	
41	The warning interval 68 is the technical product of the ordering of the two levels, and it is the point of the arrangement. 42

Defining the warning vacuum level 64 with respect to the release vacuum level 66 is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.
46	
47	In embodiments, the warning indicator 32 remains active for as long as the grip vacuum remains at or below the warning vacuum level 64, and deactivates only when the grip vacuum returns above the warning vacuum level 64. A decaying grip therefore produces a warning that persists and grows more urgent in context rather than a single transient that a user in a noisy environment may miss.
48	
49	In embodiments, activation of the warning indicator 32 at the warning vacuum level 64 does not depend on the state of the electric vacuum pump 20. If a leak is larger than the electric vacuum pump 20 can make up, the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level 64 while the electric vacuum pump 20 is still running, and the warning indicator 32 activates then and there rather than waiting for the electric vacuum pump 20 to give up. The user is thus told about the grip, which is the thing that is failing, and is not left to infer it from the behaviour of the pump, which is not.
50	
51	In embodiments, the warning vacuum level 64 is set so that the reserve of grip between the warning vacuum level 64 and the release vacuum level 66 corresponds to the whole of the load-holding margin that the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is designed to keep for the workpiece 50 it is rated to carry: the crossing of the warning vacuum level 64 then marks the point at which the grip has ceased to be sound, not the point at which it has nearly gone.
52	
53	[DRAFTING NOTE: The disclosure does not give numerical values for the working vacuum level 62, the warning vacuum level 64, or the design margin between the warning vacuum level 64 and the release vacuum level 66, nor the rated load or the expected duration of the warning interval 68. Values, or at least a design rule for setting the warning vacuum level 64 (for example, as a stated fraction of the working vacuum level 62, or as a stated multiple of the release vacuum level 66 computed for the rated load), are needed to support numerical dependent claims. None have been invented here.]
54

56	
57	A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 5. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air from the sealed region 18 through the port 22 and establishes the grip vacuum, which is raised to the working vacuum level 62. The workpiece 50 is then lifted and carried by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the grip vacuum.
58	
59	At a monitoring step 206, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the load is retained. At a comparing step 208, the grip vacuum is compared with the warning vacuum level 64. While the grip vacuum remains above the warning vacuum level 64, the method returns to the monitoring step 206. At an activating step 210, upon the grip vacuum falling to the warning vacuum level 64, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate. Because the warning vacuum level 64 is greater than the release vacuum level 66, the activating step 210 occurs while the suction cup 10 still retains the load and before the grip vacuum has fallen to the release vacuum level 66. At a maintaining step 212, the warning indicator 32 is kept active for as long as the grip vacuum remains at or below the warning vacuum level 64, while the user, within the warning interval 68, sets the workpiece 50 down.
60	
61	The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. Terms such as upper, lower, above, and below are used with reference to the orientation shown in the drawings and do not restrict the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 to any particular attitude in use. 1	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter has a rigid body with a handle and a suction cup carried by the rigid body. A flexible sealing lip of the suction cup bounds a sealed region against a workpiece such as a glass or stone panel. An electric vacuum pump within the rigid body draws air from the sealed region through a port to establish a grip vacuum that retains a load, a pressure sensor monitors the grip vacuum, and a rechargeable battery carried by the rigid body powers the pump. A warning indicator on the rigid body, driven by the pressure sensor, activates when the grip vacuum falls to a warning vacuum level that is greater than the release vacuum level at which the suction cup would let go, so the user is warned while the cup is still holding the load.

Hand-carried suction devices that signal something about their own state are also known. A sucker for plate glass has been described having a sucker body defining a suction hole at a suction surface, a manually operatable vacuum pump carried on the body, a sensor communicating with the suction channel that connects the suction hole at the suction surface with the suction hole in the pump, and a sound generator that is turned on through a switch closed by the sensor when the degree of vacuum sensed reaches a predetermined value [REF:US-5184858-A]. The pump in that device is worked by hand rather than electrically, and the sound is generated at a predetermined degree of vacuum which the reference does not relate to the vacuum still needed to retain the sheet.

A portable hand grab has been described including one or more suction cups, at least one handle connected to the suction cups for gripping by hand, at least one electrical vacuum pump for at least partially evacuating the suction volume between the suction cups and the attachment surfaces, at least one vacuum sensor for detecting a vacuum level in the suction volume, and an electronic controller configured to control the pump to at least partially evacuate the suction volume when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being less than a preselected minimum vacuum level, optionally together with an attach indicator that the controller activates when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being greater than a preselected safe vacuum level [REF:WO-2017156581-A1]. The signal there tells the user that the vacuum is high enough to attach, and a vacuum below the preselected minimum vacuum level is answered by running the pump again rather than by telling the user that the grip is going.

A cordless wand device for grasping objects such as silicon wafers has been described having a housing with a hollow interior, a tip attached to the housing through a hollow tube and having a perimeter region contoured to form an airtight seal against the object, a power source and a vacuum pump positioned within the housing, and light-emitting diodes of different colours which indicate to an operator whether the power source is sufficiently charged to generate sufficient suction force to safely grasp the object, that sufficiency being determined from the voltage drop across resistors connected across the power source [REF:US-5374090-A]. What is indicated in that device is the state of the power source rather than the state of the grip on the object.

A portable electric carrying suction cup structure has been described in which a handle is fixed on the upper end of the suction cup body, a vacuum pump is provided on the suction cup body, and a control unit is connected between the power supply part and the vacuum pump, so that air continues to be pumped out after the suction cup body and the material surface have reached an airtight state; the control unit is provided with a pressure gauge by which the user can know the pressure change between the suction cup body and the surface, with a light source for displaying different usage states, and with a buzzer for sending out alarm sounds according to different usage states [REF:CN-2806399-Y]. That reference attributes the avoidance of loosening and falling during movement to the continued pumping, and it describes the buzzer as sounding according to different usage states without relating any sounding condition to the vacuum at which the cup would let go of the material.

A digital display suction cup has been described comprising a suction cup and a handle structure, the two ends of the handle structure being provided with a switch button and a pressure relief valve, the handle structure being provided with a battery and a vacuum electric pump which is connected to the suction cup through an air pipe, with an air pressure sensor and a display screen at the lower part of the battery end, a USB charging port electrically connected to the battery, and an inner side of the suction cup provided with an evacuation hole, a pressure relief hole, and a sensing through hole [REF:US-2024424646-A1]. That device monitors and maintains negative pressure in real time and shows the negative pressure value and the battery power on the display screen as numbers for the user to read.

tool_use_result.originalFile:
A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to move glass panes, stone slabs, and similar flat panels on site by suction gripping. A suction cup is pressed against the face of the panel, air is removed from the space enclosed between the cup and the panel, and the resulting difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in that enclosed space clamps the cup to the panel so that the panel can be carried.

A suction grip is only as good as its seal. Dust on the panel, a textured or porous surface, a nick in the sealing lip, a change in temperature, or simply the slow permeation and leakage that occurs over minutes of handling will all bleed air back into the enclosed space. As air returns, the clamping force falls. The failure is progressive and, from the point of view of the person holding the panel, silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes until the cup lets go, at which point a heavy panel is already falling.

Vacuum lifting equipment has therefore long been fitted with vacuum monitoring. In one known lifter for transporting loads having an adhesion surface, a suction plate assembly carries projecting annular seals defining a vacuum chamber connected to a main vacuum source, a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that can be started by an emergency switch is additionally provided, and a pressure pickup associated with the vacuum chamber is coupled with a malfunction alarm such that the alarm is turned on when a preset limit pressure is exceeded during vacuum operation [REF:US-5310232-A]. That equipment is a suspended plate assembly with a main vacuum source and a separate emergency vacuum source; the alarm is described as a malfunction alarm tied to a preset limit pressure, and the reference does not describe the limit pressure in terms of the vacuum still needed to keep hold of the load.

Control systems for vacuum lift equipment have also been described in which a programmable controller interprets feedback from vacuum level sensors and battery sensors and responsively provides warnings and limits or alters machine functions, including evaluating a change in measured vacuum level over time to determine a rate of vacuum level change that may be caused by a leak and outputting a warning indication when that rate exceeds a threshold rate [REF:US-10518985-B2]. Such a system is built around a controller with memory, stored records, and machine-function interlocks, and its leak warning is a response to how fast the vacuum is changing rather than to where the vacuum sits relative to the point at which the grip would fail.

Powered suction devices in a hand-carried format are also known. An electric vacuum suction lifter has been described having a main body with a suction surface carrying first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space, a control unit, a vacuum pump controlled by the control unit to draw air from the sealed space, a pressure sensing unit that measures the pressure of the sealed space to generate instant pressure information, a battery unit that is charged by external power equipment and powers the control unit, pump, and pressure sensing unit, a start button, a pressure relief button, and at least one handle by which a member gripped by the device can be carried [REF:US-10625955-B2]. In that device the instant pressure information is compared with a high predetermined pressure and a low predetermined pressure: reaching the high predetermined pressure stops the pump, and falling below the low predetermined pressure restarts the pump. A warning unit is described as being operated when the detected battery power is below a predetermined battery power, and warning information relating to pressure is described as being transmitted to an external electronic device. A closely similar electric suction cup has likewise been described, in which the pressure detection unit detects the pressure between the suction cup and the component in real time and the vacuum pump automatically acts again when that pressure is lower than a second predetermined pressure [REF:CN-110630621-B].

Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1].

Two shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and the low pressure value at which it acts is chosen with reference to the working vacuum, not with reference to how much grip is left. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone. Second, where a warning is given, it is given either on a condition unrelated to grip (battery state), on a rate of change, or at a preset limit whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established. None of these guarantees the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.

There remains a need for a self-contained, cordless, hand-held vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing at a point on the decay curve at which the grip has not yet failed.

input.new_string:
Three shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and the low pressure value at which it acts is chosen with reference to the working vacuum, not with reference to how much grip is left. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone. Second, where a signal is given, it is given on a condition unrelated to grip (battery state), on a rate of change, on a preset limit whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established, as a confirmation that the vacuum is high enough to attach, or as a number on a display which the user must look at and interpret while carrying a panel. None of these delivers the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.

Third, the equipment that has the most elaborate response to a failing grip is the equipment that is not carried in the hand. A suspended or frame-mounted assembly can cut in a second vacuum source or refuse further motion, and a device whose pump hangs on a hose or on a separate handle structure has that pipework as part of the volume it must evacuate. A lifter that is carried in one hand up a ladder, with no hose, no cord, and no external controller, has none of those remedies available to it: the only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle, and that person can only act if the notice arrives early enough.

There remains a need for a self-contained, cordless, hand-held vacuum lifter that carries its pump, its sensing, its warning, and its power supply in one body, and that tells the user that the grip is failing at a point on the decay curve at which the grip has not yet failed.

This summary introduces a selection of concepts that are described further in the detailed description. It is not intended to identify essential features of the claimed subject matter, nor to limit the scope of the claims.

A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is disclosed. The lifter has a rigid body comprising a handle, and a suction cup carried by the rigid body. The suction cup comprises a flexible sealing lip which, when placed against a workpiece, bounds a sealed region between the suction cup and the workpiece. An electric vacuum pump is disposed within the rigid body and draws air from the sealed region through a port so as to establish a grip vacuum in the sealed region, the grip vacuum holding the suction cup, and hence a load carried by the suction cup, against the workpiece. A pressure sensor monitors the grip vacuum. A warning indicator is carried by the rigid body and is driven by the pressure sensor. A rechargeable battery carried by the rigid body powers the electric vacuum pump.

The grip vacuum is treated throughout this disclosure as a positive magnitude: it is the amount by which the pressure in the sealed region is below the ambient pressure outside the lifter, so that a larger grip vacuum means a firmer grip and a decaying grip is a falling grip vacuum.

The warning indicator activates when the grip vacuum falls to a warning vacuum level. The warning vacuum level is not the level at which the grip fails and is not the level at which the pump is asked to run again. It is a level that is greater than a release vacuum level, the release vacuum level being the grip vacuum below which the suction cup can no longer retain the load. Because the warning vacuum level is above the release vacuum level, the grip vacuum on a decaying grip reaches the warning vacuum level first and the release vacuum level only afterwards. The warning indicator therefore activates while the suction cup is still holding the load, and there is grip in reserve at the moment the user is told. That reserve is what the user spends in getting the panel onto a stand, against a wall, or back onto the stack.

This ordering of levels is what makes the alarm useful in a hand-held tool rather than merely informative. A frame-mounted or suspended lifter can respond to a failing grip by itself, by cutting in a second vacuum source or by refusing to move. A cordless handheld lifter has no such recourse: the only actuator available is the person holding the handle, and a person needs an interval in which to act. Defining the warning threshold with respect to the release vacuum level, rather than with respect to the working vacuum level or with respect to a rate of change, is what makes that interval exist by construction rather than by luck.

In embodiments, the warning indicator remains active for as long as the grip vacuum stays at or below the warning vacuum level, so that a grip which is decaying continuously produces a warning which persists rather than a single transient. In embodiments, the warning indicator is positioned on the rigid body where it is perceptible to a user whose hand is on the handle and whose eyes are on the panel. In embodiments, the pressure sensor is in fluid communication with the sealed region, so that what is monitored is the grip vacuum acting on the workpiece itself rather than a proxy elsewhere in the machine.

A method of lifting a workpiece with such a lifter is also disclosed. In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

Terminology used in this disclosure has the following meanings. The grip vacuum is the amount by which the absolute pressure within the sealed region 18 is below the ambient atmospheric pressure surrounding the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, expressed as a positive magnitude. A grip vacuum of zero corresponds to no grip at all; the grip vacuum rises as air is removed from the sealed region 18 and falls as air leaks back into it. Statements that the grip vacuum is greater, higher, or above a stated level therefore mean that the pressure difference clamping the suction cup 10 to the workpiece 50 is larger, and that the grip is firmer; statements that one level is less than another mean that the pressure difference at that level is the smaller of the two. This convention is used consistently in the description, in the drawings, and in the claims.

The release vacuum level 66 is the grip vacuum below which the suction cup 10 can no longer retain the load it is carrying, that is, the grip vacuum at which the holding force produced across the area bounded by the flexible sealing lip 12 ceases to exceed the force tending to separate the suction cup 10 from the workpiece 50. The release vacuum level 66 is a property of the particular combination of suction cup 10, workpiece 50, load, and orientation in use, and it is not a setting of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The warning vacuum level 64, by contrast, is a property of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100: it is the grip vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. In the illustrated embodiment the handle 16 is an arch standing above an upper side of the rigid body 14 and the suction cup 10 depends from a lower side of the rigid body 14, so that the whole of the load hangs below the user's hand and the line of action of the load passes through the handle 16. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped on its face by the flexible sealing lip 12 of the suction cup 10 and is carried in one hand by the handle 16. A warning indicator 32 is carried on an outer surface of the rigid body 14, adjacent the handle 16, where it is perceptible to a user who is gripping the handle 16 and whose attention is on the workpiece 50 and the surroundings rather than on the tool.

The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is a single hand-held unit. Every element of it, including the elements described below that establish the grip vacuum, monitor the grip vacuum, and activate the warning indicator 32, is carried by the rigid body 14, so that the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 works without connection to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14. Nothing hangs from it and nothing has to be plugged into it while a panel is being carried, and it can be taken up a ladder or onto a scaffold in one hand.

FIG. 2 is a vertical sectional view of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 taken on line 2-2 of FIG. 1. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12 which projects toward the workpiece 50 and runs around the periphery of the suction cup 10. When the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the workpiece 50 it deflects and conforms to the face of the workpiece 50, and the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, and the face of the workpiece 50 together bound a sealed region 18. The flexible sealing lip 12 is the only part of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 that touches the workpiece 50 in normal use, and its compliance is what allows the sealed region 18 to be closed against a face that is not perfectly flat or perfectly clean. A port 22 opens into the sealed region 18 through the suction cup 10, and the rigid body 14, from which the handle 16 rises, is hollow and defines an interior cavity above the suction cup 10.

FIG. 3 is an enlarged sectional detail of the interior of the rigid body 14. An electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14 and is configured to draw air from the sealed region through the port 22. A suction passage 24 within the rigid body 14 connects the port 22 to an inlet of the electric vacuum pump 20, and air drawn through the electric vacuum pump 20 is discharged to atmosphere through an exhaust outlet 26 in the rigid body 14. A pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the grip vacuum and is in fluid communication with the sealed region by way of a sensing passage 34 that branches from the suction passage 24 on the sealed-region side of the electric vacuum pump 20, so that the pressure sensor 30 sees the pressure in the sealed region itself and not a pressure developed elsewhere in the machine. What is monitored is thus the grip actually acting on the workpiece. A rechargeable battery 40 is carried within the rigid body 14 and supplies the electric vacuum pump 20. Other sensing locations may be used, the pressure sensor 30 being placed anywhere in fluid communication with the sealed region, and the pressure sensor 30 may be of any type able to report the grip vacuum over the range between atmospheric pressure and the working vacuum level 62, whether as a continuously varying signal or as a state that changes at a set level.

Running the electric vacuum pump 20 removes air from the sealed region 18 and so raises the grip vacuum; the pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50.

Because the electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14 rather than mounted remotely and connected by a hose or an air pipe to a separate handle structure, the whole of the evacuated volume is short and small: it consists of the sealed region 18, the port 22, and the suction passage 24. A small evacuated volume matters to the behaviour described below, because it means that a leak of a given size produces a rapid and therefore detectable fall in the grip vacuum rather than a slow drift buffered by a large reservoir.

FIG. 4 shows the sensing, warning, and power arrangement schematically. The pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 over a drive path 36 that includes a threshold circuit 38. The threshold circuit 38 compares the grip vacuum reported by the pressure sensor 30 with the warning vacuum level 64 and energizes the warning indicator 32 when the grip vacuum has fallen to the warning vacuum level 64. The comparison may be made by any element that resolves the monitored grip vacuum against the warning vacuum level 64 and drives the warning indicator 32 on the result, and the warning vacuum level 64 may be established when the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is built or may be settable in service. A rechargeable battery 40 supplies the electric vacuum pump 20, the pressure sensor 30, the threshold circuit 38, and the warning indicator 32 over a power path 44, so that the monitoring and warning function is available whenever the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is in the user's hand. A charging interface 42 on the rigid body 14 receives charging power for the rechargeable battery 40 from a source external to the rigid body 14 between uses.

The warning indicator 32 is an element that a user perceives while carrying a panel, and may be of any modality or combination of modalities that reaches a user whose hand is on the handle 16 and whose eyes are on the panel.

FIG. 5 is a graph in which grip vacuum is plotted on a vacuum axis 70 against time on a time axis 72. A grip vacuum trace 60 shows the history of a grip that begins sound and then decays, a working vacuum level 62, a warning vacuum level 64, and a release vacuum level 66 are drawn across the graph at three heights, and a warning interval 68 is dimensioned along the time axis 72.

In use, the electric vacuum pump 20 first raises the grip vacuum to the working vacuum level 62, which is the grip vacuum at which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is fit to lift. The user then lifts and carries the workpiece 50. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect - because of dust or grit under the lip, a textured or porous face, a damaged lip, or flexing of the workpiece 50 - air bleeds into the sealed region 18 and the grip vacuum trace 60 falls away from the working vacuum level 62.

Two levels lie below the working vacuum level 62 on the vacuum axis 70, both of them less than the working vacuum level 62. The lower of the two is the release vacuum level 66, at which the suction cup 10 lets go. The higher of the two is the warning vacuum level 64, at which the warning indicator 32 activates. Because the warning vacuum level 64 is greater than the release vacuum level 66, a falling grip vacuum trace 60 crosses the warning vacuum level 64 before it reaches the release vacuum level 66. The warning indicator 32 therefore activates at a moment when the grip vacuum is still above the release vacuum level 66 and the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load. The elapsed time between the crossing of the warning vacuum level 64 and the arrival of the grip vacuum trace 60 at the release vacuum level 66 is the warning interval 68.

The warning interval 68 is the technical product of the ordering of the two levels, and it is the point of the arrangement. During the warning interval 68, and after the warning indicator 32 has activated, the user still has a held load and a working grip, and can walk the workpiece 50 to a stand, set it against a wall, or lower it onto the stack. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 needs to intervene, and nothing needs to be fast: the reserve of grip between the warning vacuum level 64 and the release vacuum level 66 is what buys the time, and it exists by construction because of where the warning vacuum level 64 has been set.

This is a different design decision from choosing a low pressure value at which to run a pump again. A restart threshold is chosen with reference to the working vacuum level 62: it is placed just below the working vacuum level 62 so that the grip is topped up frequently and the pump cycles little. Such a threshold says nothing about how much grip remains, and a device that responds to crossing it by running its pump will, when the leak exceeds the pump's capacity, run the pump all the way down through the release vacuum level 66 without ever telling the user that the grip is going. The warning vacuum level 64 is instead chosen with reference to the release vacuum level 66, from below the working vacuum level 62 and above the point of failure, precisely so that its crossing carries the meaning that the grip is failing and the user still has hold of the panel. It is also a different decision from warning on a rate of change: a rate-of-change warning fires on a fast leak regardless of how much grip is left, and stays silent on a slow leak that has nonetheless eaten all the reserve. And it is a different decision from reporting the grip vacuum as a number or as a confirmation that the grip is presently sound, either of which leaves the user to judge, while carrying a panel, how much of the margin has already gone.

The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool than for equipment on a frame or a boom. Frame-mounted and suspended lifters can be given their own remedies for a failing grip: a second vacuum source, a reservoir, an interlock that refuses further motion. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 that works without connection to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14 has none of these. The only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle 16, and a person needs to be told while there is still something to be done. Self-containment and the placement of the warning vacuum level 64 are therefore two halves of one design: because the tool carries no external remedy, the interval given to the user is the whole of the remedy, and defining the warning vacuum level 64 with respect to the release vacuum level 66 is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.

In embodiments, the warning indicator 32 remains active for as long as the grip vacuum remains at or below the warning vacuum level 64, and deactivates only when the grip vacuum returns above the warning vacuum level 64. A decaying grip therefore produces a warning that persists and grows more urgent in context rather than a single transient that a user in a noisy environment may miss.

In embodiments, activation of the warning indicator 32 at the warning vacuum level 64 occurs irrespective of whether the electric vacuum pump 20 is operating, and continued operation of the electric vacuum pump 20 does not suppress activation of the warning indicator 32. If a leak is larger than the electric vacuum pump 20 can make up, the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level 64 while the electric vacuum pump 20 is still running and still drawing air from the sealed region 18, and the warning indicator 32 activates then and there rather than waiting for the electric vacuum pump 20 to give up. The user is thus told about the grip, which is the thing that is failing, and is not left to infer it from the behaviour of the pump, which is not.

In embodiments, the warning vacuum level 64 is set so that the reserve of grip between the warning vacuum level 64 and the release vacuum level 66 corresponds to the whole of the load-holding margin that the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is designed to keep for the workpiece 50 it is rated to carry: the crossing of the warning vacuum level 64 then marks the point at which the grip has ceased to be sound, not the point at which it has nearly gone.

In embodiments, the suction cup 10 and the flexible sealing lip 12 are configured to seal against a planar glass or stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 conforming to the panel face under the clamping pressure produced by the grip vacuum, the workpiece 50 being a planar glass or stone panel. Such panels are the workpieces for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended: they are heavy, they are usually carried in a near-vertical attitude in which the grip is loaded in shear as well as in tension, and they break when dropped.

The dimensions of the rigid body 14, the diameter of the suction cup 10, the rated load, the materials of the rigid body 14 and of the flexible sealing lip 12, the capacity and chemistry of the rechargeable battery 40, and the numerical values of the working vacuum level 62 and the warning vacuum level 64 are selected according to the size and weight of the workpiece 50 to be carried. The flexible sealing lip 12 is of a material compliant enough to conform to the panel face and to hold that conformity while the load is carried; the rechargeable battery 40 is of a capacity sufficient to raise the grip vacuum to the working vacuum level 62 and to keep the pressure sensor 30 and the warning indicator 32 alive for the working period between charges; and the warning vacuum level 64 is set, for the rated load, above the release vacuum level 66 computed for that load, by the reserve of grip described above.

FIG. 6 is a flow diagram of a method of lifting a workpiece with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter, the method comprising a placing step 202, an evacuating step 204, a monitoring step 206, a comparing step 208, an activating step 210, and a maintaining step 212.

At the placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the workpiece 50, so that the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, and the face bound the sealed region 18. At the evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air from the sealed region 18 through the port 22 and establishes the grip vacuum, which is raised to the working vacuum level 62. The workpiece 50 is then lifted and carried in one hand by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the grip vacuum and the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 being without connection to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14.

At the monitoring step 206, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the load is retained. At the comparing step 208, the grip vacuum is compared with the warning vacuum level 64. While the grip vacuum remains above the warning vacuum level 64, the method returns to the monitoring step 206. At the activating step 210, upon the grip vacuum falling to the warning vacuum level 64, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate. Because the warning vacuum level 64 is greater than the release vacuum level 66, the activating step 210 occurs while the suction cup 10 still retains the load and before the grip vacuum has fallen to the release vacuum level 66. At the maintaining step 212, after the activating step 210, the warning indicator 32 is kept active for as long as the grip vacuum remains at or below the warning vacuum level 64, while the user, within the warning interval 68, sets the workpiece 50 down.

The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. Terms such as upper, lower, above, and below are used with reference to the orientation shown in the drawings and do not restrict the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 to any particular attitude in use. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.

FIG. 2 is a vertical sectional view of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 taken on line 2-2 of FIG. 1. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12 which projects toward the workpiece 50 and runs around the periphery of the suction cup 10. When the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the workpiece 50 it deflects and conforms to the face of the workpiece 50, and the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, and the face of the workpiece 50 together bound a sealed region 18. The flexible sealing lip 12 is the only part of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 that touches the workpiece 50 in normal use, and its compliance is what allows the sealed region 18 to be closed against a face that is not perfectly flat or perfectly clean. A port 22 opens into the sealed region 18 through the suction cup 10, and the rigid body 14, from which the handle 16 rises, is hollow and defines an interior cavity above the suction cup 10.

FIG. 3 is an enlarged sectional detail of the interior of the rigid body 14. An electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14 and is configured to draw air from the sealed region through the port 22. A suction passage 24 within the rigid body 14 connects the port 22 to an inlet of the electric vacuum pump 20, and air drawn through the electric vacuum pump 20 is discharged to atmosphere through an exhaust outlet 26 in the rigid body 14. A pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the grip vacuum and is in fluid communication with the sealed region by way of a sensing passage 34 that branches from the suction passage 24 on the sealed-region side of the electric vacuum pump 20, so that the pressure sensor 30 sees the pressure in the sealed region itself and not a pressure developed elsewhere in the machine. What is monitored is thus the grip actually acting on the workpiece. A rechargeable battery 40 is carried within the rigid body 14 and supplies the electric vacuum pump 20. Other sensing locations may be used, the pressure sensor 30 being placed anywhere in fluid communication with the sealed region, and the pressure sensor 30 may be of any type able to report the grip vacuum over the range between atmospheric pressure and the working vacuum level 62, whether as a continuously varying signal or as a state that changes at a set level.

Running the electric vacuum pump 20 removes air from the sealed region 18 and so raises the grip vacuum; the pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50.

Because the electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14 rather than mounted remotely and connected by a hose or an air pipe to a separate handle structure, the whole of the evacuated volume is short and small: it consists of the sealed region 18, the port 22, and the suction passage 24. A small evacuated volume matters to the behaviour described below, because it means that a leak of a given size produces a rapid and therefore detectable fall in the grip vacuum rather than a slow drift buffered by a large reservoir.

FIG. 4 shows the sensing, warning, and power arrangement schematically. The pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 over a drive path 36 that includes a threshold circuit 38. The threshold circuit 38 compares the grip vacuum reported by the pressure sensor 30 with the warning vacuum level 64 and energizes the warning indicator 32 when the grip vacuum has fallen to the warning vacuum level 64. The comparison may be made by any element that resolves the monitored grip vacuum against the warning vacuum level 64 and drives the warning indicator 32 on the result, and the warning vacuum level 64 may be established when the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is built or may be settable in service. A rechargeable battery 40 supplies the electric vacuum pump 20, the pressure sensor 30, the threshold circuit 38, and the warning indicator 32 over a power path 44, so that the monitoring and warning function is available whenever the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is in the user's hand. A charging interface 42 on the rigid body 14 receives charging power for the rechargeable battery 40 from a source external to the rigid body 14 between uses.

The warning indicator 32 is an element that a user perceives while carrying a panel, and may be of any modality or combination of modalities that reaches a user whose hand is on the handle 16 and whose eyes are on the panel.

FIG. 5 is a graph in which grip vacuum is plotted on a vacuum axis 70 against time on a time axis 72. A grip vacuum trace 60 shows the history of a grip that begins sound and then decays, a working vacuum level 62, a warning vacuum level 64, and a release vacuum level 66 are drawn across the graph at three heights, and a warning interval 68 is dimensioned along the time axis 72.

In use, the electric vacuum pump 20 first raises the grip vacuum to the working vacuum level 62, which is the grip vacuum at which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is fit to lift. The user then lifts and carries the workpiece 50. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect - because of dust or grit under the lip, a textured or porous face, a damaged lip, or flexing of the workpiece 50 - air bleeds into the sealed region 18 and the grip vacuum trace 60 falls away from the working vacuum level 62.

Two levels lie below the working vacuum level 62 on the vacuum axis 70, both of them less than the working vacuum level 62. The lower of the two is the release vacuum level 66, at which the suction cup 10 lets go. The higher of the two is the warning vacuum level 64, at which the warning indicator 32 activates. Because the warning vacuum level 64 is greater than the release vacuum level 66, a falling grip vacuum trace 60 crosses the warning vacuum level 64 before it reaches the release vacuum level 66. The warning indicator 32 therefore activates at a moment when the grip vacuum is still above the release vacuum level 66 and the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load. The elapsed time between the crossing of the warning vacuum level 64 and the arrival of the grip vacuum trace 60 at the release vacuum level 66 is the warning interval 68.

The warning interval 68 is the technical product of the ordering of the two levels, and it is the point of the arrangement. During the warning interval 68, and after the warning indicator 32 has activated, the user still has a held load and a working grip, and can walk the workpiece 50 to a stand, set it against a wall, or lower it onto the stack. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 needs to intervene, and nothing needs to be fast: the reserve of grip between the warning vacuum level 64 and the release vacuum level 66 is what buys the time, and it exists by construction because of where the warning vacuum level 64 has been set.

This is a different design decision from choosing a low pressure value at which to run a pump again. A restart threshold is chosen with reference to the working vacuum level 62: it is placed just below the working vacuum level 62 so that the grip is topped up frequently and the pump cycles little. Such a threshold says nothing about how much grip remains, and a device that responds to crossing it by running its pump will, when the leak exceeds the pump's capacity, run the pump all the way down through the release vacuum level 66 without ever telling the user that the grip is going. The warning vacuum level 64 is instead chosen with reference to the release vacuum level 66, from below the working vacuum level 62 and above the point of failure, precisely so that its crossing carries the meaning that the grip is failing and the user still has hold of the panel. It is also a different decision from warning on a rate of change: a rate-of-change warning fires on a fast leak regardless of how much grip is left, and stays silent on a slow leak that has nonetheless eaten all the reserve. And it is a different decision from reporting the grip vacuum as a number or as a confirmation that the grip is presently sound, either of which leaves the user to judge, while carrying a panel, how much of the margin has already gone.

The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool than for equipment on a frame or a boom. Frame-mounted and suspended lifters can be given their own remedies for a failing grip: a second vacuum source, a reservoir, an interlock that refuses further motion. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 that works without connection to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14 has none of these. The only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle 16, and a person needs to be told while there is still something to be done. Self-containment and the placement of the warning vacuum level 64 are therefore two halves of one design: because the tool carries no external remedy, the interval given to the user is the whole of the remedy, and defining the warning vacuum level 64 with respect to the release vacuum level 66 is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.

In embodiments, the warning indicator 32 remains active for as long as the grip vacuum remains at or below the warning vacuum level 64, and deactivates only when the grip vacuum returns above the warning vacuum level 64. A decaying grip therefore produces a warning that persists and grows more urgent in context rather than a single transient that a user in a noisy environment may miss.

In embodiments, activation of the warning indicator 32 at the warning vacuum level 64 occurs irrespective of whether the electric vacuum pump 20 is operating, and continued operation of the electric vacuum pump 20 does not suppress activation of the warning indicator 32. If a leak is larger than the electric vacuum pump 20 can make up, the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level 64 while the electric vacuum pump 20 is still running and still drawing air from the sealed region 18, and the warning indicator 32 activates then and there rather than waiting for the electric vacuum pump 20 to give up. The user is thus told about the grip, which is the thing that is failing, and is not left to infer it from the behaviour of the pump, which is not.

In embodiments, the warning vacuum level 64 is set so that the reserve of grip between the warning vacuum level 64 and the release vacuum level 66 corresponds to the whole of the load-holding margin that the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is designed to keep for the workpiece 50 it is rated to carry: the crossing of the warning vacuum level 64 then marks the point at which the grip has ceased to be sound, not the point at which it has nearly gone.

In embodiments, the suction cup 10 and the flexible sealing lip 12 are configured to seal against a planar glass or stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 conforming to the panel face under the clamping pressure produced by the grip vacuum, the workpiece 50 being a planar glass or stone panel. Such panels are the workpieces for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended: they are heavy, they are usually carried in a near-vertical attitude in which the grip is loaded in shear as well as in tension, and they break when dropped.

The dimensions of the rigid body 14, the diameter of the suction cup 10, the rated load, the materials of the rigid body 14 and of the flexible sealing lip 12, the capacity and chemistry of the rechargeable battery 40, and the numerical values of the working vacuum level 62 and the warning vacuum level 64 are selected according to the size and weight of the workpiece 50 to be carried. The flexible sealing lip 12 is of a material compliant enough to conform to the panel face and to hold that conformity while the load is carried; the rechargeable battery 40 is of a capacity sufficient to raise the grip vacuum to the working vacuum level 62 and to keep the pressure sensor 30 and the warning indicator 32 alive for the working period between charges; and the warning vacuum level 64 is set, for the rated load, above the release vacuum level 66 computed for that load, by the reserve of grip described above.

FIG. 6 is a flow diagram of a method of lifting a workpiece with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter, the method comprising a placing step 202, an evacuating step 204, a monitoring step 206, a comparing step 208, an activating step 210, and a maintaining step 212.

At the placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the workpiece 50, so that the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, and the face bound the sealed region 18. At the evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air from the sealed region 18 through the port 22 and establishes the grip vacuum, which is raised to the working vacuum level 62. The workpiece 50 is then lifted and carried in one hand by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the grip vacuum and the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 being without connection to any hose, cord, or controller external to the rigid body 14.

At the monitoring step 206, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the load is retained. At the comparing step 208, the grip vacuum is compared with the warning vacuum level 64. While the grip vacuum remains above the warning vacuum level 64, the method returns to the monitoring step 206. At the activating step 210, upon the grip vacuum falling to the warning vacuum level 64, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate. Because the warning vacuum level 64 is greater than the release vacuum level 66, the activating step 210 occurs while the suction cup 10 still retains the load and before the grip vacuum has fallen to the release vacuum level 66. At the maintaining step 212, after the activating step 210, the warning indicator 32 is kept active for as long as the grip vacuum remains at or below the warning vacuum level 64, while the user, within the warning interval 68, sets the workpiece 50 down.

A grip vacuum trace 60 shows the history of a grip that begins sound and then decays, a working vacuum level 62, a warning vacuum level 64, and a release vacuum level 66 are drawn across the graph at three heights, and a warning interval 68 is dimensioned along the time axis 72.

Two levels lie below the working vacuum level 62 on the vacuum axis 70, both of them less than the working vacuum level 62. The lower of the two is the release vacuum level 66, at which the suction cup 10 lets go. The higher of the two is the warning vacuum level 64, at which the warning indicator 32 activates. Because the warning vacuum level 64 is greater than the release vacuum level 66, a falling grip vacuum trace 60 crosses the warning vacuum level 64 before it reaches the release vacuum level 66. The warning indicator 32 therefore activates at a moment when the grip vacuum is still above the release vacuum level 66 and the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load. The elapsed time between the crossing of the warning vacuum level 64 and the arrival of the grip vacuum trace 60 at the release vacuum level 66 is the warning interval 68.

The warning interval 68 is the technical product of the ordering of the two levels, and it is the point of the arrangement. During the warning interval 68, and after the warning indicator 32 has activated, the user still has a held load and a working grip, and can walk the workpiece 50 to a stand, set it against a wall, or lower it onto the stack. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 needs to intervene, and nothing needs to be fast: the reserve of grip between the warning vacuum level 64 and the release vacuum level 66 is what buys the time, and it exists by construction because of where the warning vacuum level 64 has been set.

This is a different design decision from choosing a low pressure value at which to run a pump again. A restart threshold is chosen with reference to the working vacuum level 62: it is placed just below the working vacuum level 62 so that the grip is topped up frequently and the pump cycles little. Such a threshold says nothing about how much grip remains, and a device that responds to crossing it by running its pump will, when the leak exceeds the pump's capacity, run the pump all the way down through the release vacuum level 66 without ever telling the user that the grip is going. The warning vacuum level 64 is instead chosen with reference to the release vacuum level 66, from below the working vacuum level 62 and above the point of failure, precisely so that its crossing carries the meaning that the grip is failing and the user still has hold of the panel. It is also a different decision from warning on a rate of change: a rate-of-change warning fires on a fast leak regardless of how much grip is left, and stays silent on a slow leak that has nonetheless eaten all the reserve. And it is a different decision from reporting the grip vacuum as a number or as a confirmation that the grip is presently sound, either of which leaves the user to judge, while carrying a panel, how much of the margin has already gone.
