tool_use_result.originalFile:
A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to move glass panes, stone slabs, and similar flat panels on site by suction gripping. A suction cup is pressed against the face of the panel, air is removed from the space enclosed between the cup and the panel, and the resulting difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in that enclosed space clamps the cup to the panel so that the panel can be carried.

A suction grip is only as good as its seal. Dust on the panel, a textured or porous surface, a nick in the sealing lip, a change in temperature, or simply the slow permeation and leakage that occurs over minutes of handling will all bleed air back into the enclosed space. As air returns, the clamping force falls. The failure is progressive and, from the point of view of the person holding the panel, silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes until the cup lets go, at which point a heavy panel is already falling.

Vacuum lifting equipment has therefore long been fitted with vacuum monitoring. In one known lifter for transporting loads having an adhesion surface, a suction plate assembly carries projecting annular seals defining a vacuum chamber connected to a main vacuum source, a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that can be started by an emergency switch is additionally provided, and a pressure pickup associated with the vacuum chamber is coupled with a malfunction alarm such that the alarm is turned on when a preset limit pressure is exceeded during vacuum operation [REF:US-5310232-A]. That equipment is a suspended plate assembly with a main vacuum source and a separate emergency vacuum source; the alarm is described as a malfunction alarm tied to a preset limit pressure, and the reference does not describe the limit pressure in terms of the vacuum still needed to keep hold of the load.

Control systems for vacuum lift equipment have also been described in which a programmable controller interprets feedback from vacuum level sensors and battery sensors and responsively provides warnings and limits or alters machine functions, including evaluating a change in measured vacuum level over time to determine a rate of vacuum level change that may be caused by a leak and outputting a warning indication when that rate exceeds a threshold rate [REF:US-10518985-B2]. Such a system is built around a controller with memory, stored records, and machine-function interlocks, and its leak warning is a response to how fast the vacuum is changing rather than to where the vacuum sits relative to the point at which the grip would fail.

Powered suction devices in a hand-carried format are also known. An electric vacuum suction lifter has been described having a main body with a suction surface carrying first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space, a control unit, a vacuum pump controlled by the control unit to draw air from the sealed space, a pressure sensing unit that measures the pressure of the sealed space to generate instant pressure information, a battery unit that is charged by external power equipment and powers the control unit, pump, and pressure sensing unit, a start button, a pressure relief button, and at least one handle by which a member gripped by the device can be carried [REF:US-10625955-B2]. In that device the instant pressure information is compared with a high predetermined pressure and a low predetermined pressure: reaching the high predetermined pressure stops the pump, and falling below the low predetermined pressure restarts the pump. A warning unit is described as being operated when the detected battery power is below a predetermined battery power, and warning information relating to pressure is described as being transmitted to an external electronic device. A closely similar electric suction cup has likewise been described, in which the pressure detection unit detects the pressure between the suction cup and the component in real time and the vacuum pump automatically acts again when that pressure is lower than a second predetermined pressure [REF:CN-110630621-B].

Hand-carried suction devices that signal something about their own state are also known. A sucker for plate glass has been described having a sucker body defining a suction hole at a suction surface, a manually operatable vacuum pump carried on the body, a sensor communicating with the suction channel that connects the suction hole at the suction surface with the suction hole in the pump, and a sound generator that is turned on through a switch closed by the sensor when the degree of vacuum sensed reaches a predetermined value [REF:US-5184858-A]. The pump in that device is worked by hand rather than electrically, and the sound is generated at a predetermined degree of vacuum which the reference does not relate to the vacuum still needed to retain the sheet.

A portable hand grab has been described including one or more suction cups, at least one handle connected to the suction cups for gripping by hand, at least one electrical vacuum pump for at least partially evacuating the suction volume between the suction cups and the attachment surfaces, at least one vacuum sensor for detecting a vacuum level in the suction volume, and an electronic controller configured to control the pump to at least partially evacuate the suction volume when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being less than a preselected minimum vacuum level, optionally together with an attach indicator that the controller activates when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being greater than a preselected safe vacuum level [REF:WO-2017156581-A1]. The signal there tells the user that the vacuum is high enough to attach, and a vacuum below the preselected minimum vacuum level is answered by running the pump again rather than by telling the user that the grip is going.

A cordless wand device for grasping objects such as silicon wafers has been described having a housing with a hollow interior, a tip attached to the housing through a hollow tube and having a perimeter region contoured to form an airtight seal against the object, a power source and a vacuum pump positioned within the housing, and light-emitting diodes of different colours which indicate to an operator whether the power source is sufficiently charged to generate sufficient suction force to safely grasp the object, that sufficiency being determined from the voltage drop across resistors connected across the power source [REF:US-5374090-A]. What is indicated in that device is the state of the power source rather than the state of the grip on the object.

A portable electric carrying suction cup structure has been described in which a handle is fixed on the upper end of the suction cup body, a vacuum pump is provided on the suction cup body, and a control unit is connected between the power supply part and the vacuum pump, so that air continues to be pumped out after the suction cup body and the material surface have reached an airtight state; the control unit is provided with a pressure gauge by which the user can know the pressure change between the suction cup body and the surface, with a light source for displaying different usage states, and with a buzzer for sending out alarm sounds according to different usage states [REF:CN-2806399-Y]. That reference attributes the avoidance of loosening and falling during movement to the continued pumping, and it describes the buzzer as sounding according to different usage states without relating any sounding condition to the vacuum at which the cup would let go of the material.

A digital display suction cup has been described comprising a suction cup and a handle structure, the two ends of the handle structure being provided with a switch button and a pressure relief valve, the handle structure being provided with a battery and a vacuum electric pump which is connected to the suction cup through an air pipe, with an air pressure sensor and a display screen at the lower part of the battery end, a USB charging port electrically connected to the battery, and an inner side of the suction cup provided with an evacuation hole, a pressure relief hole, and a sensing through hole [REF:US-2024424646-A1]. That device monitors and maintains negative pressure in real time and shows the negative pressure value and the battery power on the display screen as numbers for the user to read.

Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1].

Three shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and the low pressure value at which it acts is chosen with reference to the working vacuum, not with reference to how much grip is left. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone. Second, where a signal is given, it is given on a condition unrelated to grip (battery state), on a rate of change, on a preset limit whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established, as a confirmation that the vacuum is high enough to attach, or as a number on a display which the user must look at and interpret while carrying a panel. None of these delivers the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.

Third, the equipment that has the most elaborate response to a failing grip is the equipment that is not carried in the hand. A suspended or frame-mounted assembly can cut in a second vacuum source or refuse further motion, and a device whose pump hangs on a hose or on a separate handle structure has that pipework as part of the volume it must evacuate. A lifter that is carried in one hand up a ladder, with no hose, no cord, and no external controller, has none of those remedies available to it: the only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle, and that person can only act if the notice arrives early enough.

There remains a need for a self-contained, cordless, hand-held vacuum lifter that carries its pump, its sensing, its warning, and its power supply in one body, and that tells the user that the grip is failing at a point on the decay curve at which the grip has not yet failed.

content.text: Now the Summary, reduced to the disclosed ledger:

input.content:
This summary introduces a selection of concepts that are described further in the detailed description. It is not intended to identify essential features of the claimed subject matter, nor to limit the scope of the claims.

A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is disclosed. The lifter has a rigid body comprising a handle, and a suction cup carried by the rigid body. The suction cup comprises a flexible sealing lip. An electric vacuum pump is disposed within the rigid body and draws air through a port to create a grip vacuum, the grip vacuum retaining a load on the suction cup. A pressure sensor monitors the grip vacuum. A warning indicator is driven by the pressure sensor. A rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump.

The grip vacuum is treated throughout this disclosure as a positive magnitude: it is the amount by which the pressure holding the suction cup to the load is below the ambient pressure outside the lifter, so that a larger grip vacuum means a firmer grip and a decaying grip is a falling grip vacuum.

The warning indicator activates when the grip vacuum falls to a warning vacuum level. The warning vacuum level is greater than a release vacuum level, the release vacuum level being the grip vacuum below which the suction cup can no longer retain the load. Because the warning vacuum level is greater than the release vacuum level, the grip vacuum on a decaying grip reaches the warning vacuum level first and the release vacuum level only afterwards. The warning indicator therefore activates while the suction cup is still retaining the load, that is, before the load can be dropped.

This ordering of levels is what makes the alarm useful in a hand-held tool rather than merely informative. A frame-mounted or suspended lifter can respond to a failing grip by itself, by cutting in a second vacuum source or by refusing to move. A cordless handheld lifter has no such recourse: the only actuator available is the person holding the handle, and a person needs an interval in which to act. Defining the warning threshold with respect to the release vacuum level is what makes that interval exist by construction rather than by luck.

Because the rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump, the lifter grips, monitors, and warns without a cord to an external power supply.

A method of lifting a glass or stone panel with such a lifter is also disclosed. The method includes placing the flexible sealing lip against the panel, drawing air through the port with the electric vacuum pump powered by the rechargeable battery to create the grip vacuum, lifting and carrying the panel by the handle, monitoring the grip vacuum with the pressure sensor while the panel is retained on the suction cup, and activating the warning indicator when the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level, that is, while the suction cup still retains the panel and before the panel can be dropped.

In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

Terminology used in this disclosure has the following meanings. The grip vacuum is the amount by which the pressure holding the suction cup 10 to the load is below the ambient atmospheric pressure surrounding the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, expressed as a positive magnitude. A grip vacuum of zero corresponds to no grip at all; the grip vacuum rises as air is drawn away by the electric vacuum pump 20 and falls as the grip decays. Statements that the grip vacuum is greater, higher, or above a stated level therefore mean that the grip is firmer. This convention is used consistently in the description, in the drawings, and in the claims.

The release vacuum level is the grip vacuum below which the suction cup 10 can no longer retain the load it is carrying. The warning vacuum level is the grip vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. In use, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a panel 50 of glass or stone, and the panel 50 is the load which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 carries.

FIG. 2 shows the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 schematically. An electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14 and is configured to draw air through a port 22 to create a grip vacuum, by which grip vacuum the suction cup 10 retains the load. A pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the grip vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. A rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20.

The warning indicator 32 activates when the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level. Because the warning vacuum level is greater than the release vacuum level, a decaying grip vacuum reaches the warning vacuum level before it reaches the release vacuum level, and the warning indicator 32 therefore activates while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load. The user is warned before the load can be dropped, and still has a held load and a working grip at the moment of being told.

The placing of the warning vacuum level with respect to the release vacuum level is what makes the warning useful rather than merely informative, and it is a different design decision from signalling on a condition that is not related to the grip still needed to retain the load. A threshold that is placed by reference to the vacuum at which the pump is asked to run again says nothing about how much grip remains, and a warning given on how fast the vacuum is changing fires on a fast leak regardless of the grip left and stays silent on a slow leak that has consumed the same grip. Only a threshold placed above the grip vacuum at which the suction cup 10 lets go guarantees that the warning indicator 32 activates while the load is still held.

The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool than for equipment on a frame or a boom. Frame-mounted and suspended lifters can be given their own remedies for a failing grip: a second vacuum source, a reservoir, an interlock that refuses further motion. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has none of these. The only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle 16, and a person needs to be told while there is still something to be done. Defining the warning vacuum level with respect to the release vacuum level is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.

The rechargeable battery 40 is the power supply for the electric vacuum pump 20, so that the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 grips, monitors the grip vacuum, and warns without a cord to an external power supply.

The panel 50 is a glass or stone panel, of the kind moved on site by suction gripping, and the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the panel 50 when the panel 50 is to be lifted.

FIG. 3 is a flow diagram of a method of lifting the panel 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, the method comprising a placing step 202, an evacuating step 204, a monitoring step 206, and an activating step 208.

At the placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the panel 50. At the evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the grip vacuum, and the panel 50 is lifted and carried by the handle 16, the panel 50 being retained on the suction cup 10 by the grip vacuum. At the monitoring step 206, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the panel 50 is retained on the suction cup 10. At the activating step 208, upon the grip vacuum falling to the warning vacuum level, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate. Because the warning vacuum level is greater than the release vacuum level, the activating step 208 occurs while the suction cup 10 still retains the panel 50, that is, before the panel 50 can be dropped.

The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.

Terminology used in this disclosure has the following meanings. The grip vacuum is the amount by which the absolute pressure within the sealed region 18 is below the ambient atmospheric pressure surrounding the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, expressed as a positive magnitude. A grip vacuum of zero corresponds to no grip at all; the grip vacuum rises as air is removed from the sealed region 18 and falls as air leaks back into it. In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

Terminology used in this disclosure has the following meanings. The grip vacuum is the amount by which the pressure holding the suction cup 10 to the load is below the ambient atmospheric pressure surrounding the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, expressed as a positive magnitude. A grip vacuum of zero corresponds to no grip at all; the grip vacuum rises as air is drawn away by the electric vacuum pump 20 and falls as the grip decays. Statements that the grip vacuum is greater, higher, or above a stated level therefore mean that the grip is firmer. This convention is used consistently in the description, in the drawings, and in the claims.

The release vacuum level is the grip vacuum below which the suction cup 10 can no longer retain the load it is carrying. The warning vacuum level is the grip vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. In use, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a panel 50 of glass or stone, and the panel 50 is the load which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 carries.

FIG. 2 shows the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 schematically. An electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14 and is configured to draw air through a port 22 to create a grip vacuum, by which grip vacuum the suction cup 10 retains the load. A pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the grip vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. A rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20.

The warning indicator 32 activates when the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level. Because the warning vacuum level is greater than the release vacuum level, a decaying grip vacuum reaches the warning vacuum level before it reaches the release vacuum level, and the warning indicator 32 therefore activates while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load. The user is warned before the load can be dropped, and still has a held load and a working grip at the moment of being told.

In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

Terminology used in this disclosure has the following meanings. The grip vacuum is the vacuum created when the electric vacuum pump 20 draws air through the port 22, expressed as a positive magnitude: it is the amount by which the pressure of the air that has been drawn away is below the ambient atmospheric pressure surrounding the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. A grip vacuum of zero corresponds to no grip at all; the grip vacuum rises as the electric vacuum pump 20 draws air away and falls as the grip decays. Statements that the grip vacuum is greater, higher, or above a stated level therefore mean that the grip is firmer. This convention is used consistently in the description, in the drawings, and in the claims.

The release vacuum level is the grip vacuum below which the suction cup 10 can no longer retain the load it is carrying. The warning vacuum level is the grip vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. In use, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a panel 50 of glass or stone, and the panel 50 is the load which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 carries.

FIG. 2 shows schematically the suction cup 10, a port 22, an electric vacuum pump 20, a pressure sensor 30, a warning indicator 32, and a rechargeable battery 40, and the connections among them.

The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14 and is configured to draw air through the port 22 to create a grip vacuum, by which grip vacuum the suction cup 10 retains the load. The pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the grip vacuum. The warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. The rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20.

The warning indicator 32 activates when the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level. Because the warning vacuum level is greater than the release vacuum level, a decaying grip vacuum reaches the warning vacuum level before it reaches the release vacuum level, and the warning indicator 32 therefore activates while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load. The user is warned before the load can be dropped, and still has a held load and a working grip at the moment of being told.

The placing of the warning vacuum level with respect to the release vacuum level is what makes the warning useful rather than merely informative, and it is a different design decision from signalling on a condition that is not related to the grip still needed to retain the load. A threshold that is placed by reference to the vacuum at which the pump is asked to run again says nothing about how much grip remains, and a warning given on how fast the vacuum is changing fires on a fast leak regardless of the grip left and stays silent on a slow leak that has consumed the same grip. Only a threshold placed above the grip vacuum at which the suction cup 10 lets go guarantees that the warning indicator 32 activates while the load is still held.

The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool than for equipment on a frame or a boom. Frame-mounted and suspended lifters can be given their own remedies for a failing grip: a second vacuum source, a reservoir, an interlock that refuses further motion. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has none of these. The only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle 16, and a person needs to be told while there is still something to be done. Defining the warning vacuum level with respect to the release vacuum level is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.

The rechargeable battery 40 is the power supply for the electric vacuum pump 20, so that the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 grips, monitors the grip vacuum, and warns without a cord to an external power supply.

The panel 50 is a glass or stone panel, of the kind moved on site by suction gripping, and the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the panel 50 when the panel 50 is to be lifted.

FIG. 3 is a flow diagram of a method of lifting a panel with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter, the method comprising a placing step 202, an evacuating step 204, a monitoring step 206, and an activating step 208.

At the placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the panel 50. At the evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the grip vacuum, and the panel 50 is lifted and carried by the handle 16, the panel 50 being retained on the suction cup 10 by the grip vacuum. At the monitoring step 206, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the panel 50 is retained on the suction cup 10. At the activating step 208, upon the grip vacuum falling to the warning vacuum level, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate. Because the warning vacuum level is greater than the release vacuum level, the activating step 208 occurs while the suction cup 10 still retains the panel 50, that is, before the panel 50 can be dropped.

The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.

input.summary: Rebuilt the application on the inventor's ledger only. Every element the review identified as untraced is gone from the claims, the description, the numeral table and the drawings: the internal air path and exhaust, the sensing passage and plumbing point, the drive path and threshold circuit, the charging interface and power path and the battery powering anything but the pump, the whole graph apparatus of trace, axes, working level and warning interval, indicator persistence, pump-independent activation, the load-holding margin and threshold-setting rule, the indicator's position on the body, the handle-above and cup-below topology with its line of action, the self-containment clause and the "carried by the rigid body" qualifiers on the sensor and indicator, the sealed-region geometry and lip topology and port location, the comparing decision loop and the maintaining and set-down steps, the force analysis in the release-level definition, and the gap-filling breadth statements about sensor type, indicator modality and threshold implementation. The claim set is now 5 apparatus claims and 3 method claims, all recited in the words of the disclosure; the "consists of" contradiction disappeared with the passages it lived in. The drawing plan is three sheets: a shape-neutral side elevation, a schematic of the six disclosed elements and their connections, and a four-step flow diagram. The numeral table holds 15 entries, every one of them used in the text and shown on a sheet, and no sheet carries more than six numerals. The warning vacuum level and release vacuum level are retained as the reviewer's two permitted sentences and are now unnumbered terms, since the graph that carried numerals 64 and 66 is gone and no numeral may sit off the drawings.
reasoning: The claims were rewritten from the disclosure's own two claims outward. Claim 1 keeps only body and handle, cup and flexible sealing lip, pump within the body drawing air through a port to create the grip vacuum, sensor monitoring that vacuum, indicator driven by the sensor, and battery powering the pump. The single relational limitation is the one the review confirmed as traceable: the indicator activates at a warning vacuum level greater than the release vacuum level at which the cup ceases to retain the load, which is the disclosure's "warns before a load can be dropped" expressed so that it has one meaning.

The dependent ladder now contains only limitations the ledger carries: activation before the load can be dropped, the release-level definition in the reviewer's own permitted wording, operation on the rechargeable battery without a cord to an external power supply (the review states that "cordless" is affirmative support for the absence of a cord alone), and the glass or stone panel as the load. Nothing was retained merely because it was a useful fallback.

The method claim was cut to the four steps that restate disclosed apparatus functions, in the terms the review permitted: placing the lip against the panel, drawing air through the port with the pump powered by the battery, monitoring the grip vacuum with the sensor, and activating the indicator at the warning vacuum level. The comparing decision, its loop, the maintaining step and the set-down step are gone, and with them claims that rested on them.

Numerals 64 and 66 were dropped rather than kept off-drawing. The graph sheet that displayed them is deleted as unsupported, and a numeral that appears in the text but on no drawing fails a mechanical check, so the warning vacuum level and the release vacuum level are now defined terms without numerals. That keeps the two permitted definitional sentences while leaving every numeral in the table on a sheet.

The figure plan was redistributed rather than pruned of disclosed parts. FIG. 1 carries the six structural numerals with no proportion, no coaxiality, no cup profile and no panel attitude; FIG. 2 carries the six functional numerals as plain rectangles and connections with no enclosure boundary, no unnumbered air lines, no flow arrows and no stated side of any axis; FIG. 3 carries the four step numerals as empty rectangles in one column. Six, six and four numerals per sheet.

The description paragraphs that introduce each figure now name only numerals that appear on that sheet, and the structural sentences about the pump being within the rigid body sit in a following paragraph that does not reference a figure, so no part is described as visible on a sheet that does not list it.

The near-vertical attitude sentence, the shear and tension and breakage assertions and the qualifier "planar" are removed, so the workpiece is simply a glass or stone panel, matching the disclosure and matching what FIG. 1 shows. The term "workpiece" was replaced by "panel" throughout for the same reason.

What remains of the technical argument is argument about the disclosed relationship, not added structure: why a threshold placed above the vacuum at which the cup lets go warns while the load is still held, and why a hand-carried tool needs that interval when a frame-mounted one does not. No apparatus, level, value or measurement supports it that the disclosure does not supply.

The Background retains its prior-art discussion, which the review placed outside its scope, but the two sentences that projected self-containment onto the invention were reduced to the hand-carried framing and the closing need statement now asks only for a cordless hand-held lifter that warns while the cup is still holding.

input.prior_art_strategy: The Background still addresses every reference in the index, and its characterizations are unchanged. What now carries claim 1 is the single relationship the disclosure supplies and no reference states: the indicator fires at a level defined against the vacuum at which the cup ceases to retain the load, so that activation necessarily precedes release. The restart-threshold devices place their low pressure value against the working vacuum and answer it by running the pump; the controller system warns on a rate of vacuum change; the hand grab's indicator confirms that the vacuum is high enough to attach; the plate-glass sucker's sound generator fires at a predetermined degree of vacuum unrelated to retention; the wand's diodes report the charge state of the power source; the digital display cup presents pressure as a number to read. Claim 4 adds the cordless fallback, that the battery is the power supply so the lifter grips, monitors and warns without a cord to an external supply, which the disclosure's own word \"cordless\" supports. Features that would have separated the claims further, the internal ducting, the sensing point, the confined evacuated volume and full self-containment, are not in the disclosure and are therefore not claimed.

structured_output.summary: Rebuilt the application on the inventor's ledger only. Every element the review identified as untraced is gone from the claims, the description, the numeral table and the drawings: the internal air path and exhaust, the sensing passage and plumbing point, the drive path and threshold circuit, the charging interface and power path and the battery powering anything but the pump, the whole graph apparatus of trace, axes, working level and warning interval, indicator persistence, pump-independent activation, the load-holding margin and threshold-setting rule, the indicator's position on the body, the handle-above and cup-below topology with its line of action, the self-containment clause and the "carried by the rigid body" qualifiers on the sensor and indicator, the sealed-region geometry and lip topology and port location, the comparing decision loop and the maintaining and set-down steps, the force analysis in the release-level definition, and the gap-filling breadth statements about sensor type, indicator modality and threshold implementation. The claim set is now 5 apparatus claims and 3 method claims, all recited in the words of the disclosure; the "consists of" contradiction disappeared with the passages it lived in. The drawing plan is three sheets: a shape-neutral side elevation, a schematic of the six disclosed elements and their connections, and a four-step flow diagram. The numeral table holds 15 entries, every one of them used in the text and shown on a sheet, and no sheet carries more than six numerals. The warning vacuum level and release vacuum level are retained as the reviewer's two permitted sentences and are now unnumbered terms, since the graph that carried numerals 64 and 66 is gone and no numeral may sit off the drawings.
reasoning: The claims were rewritten from the disclosure's own two claims outward. Claim 1 keeps only body and handle, cup and flexible sealing lip, pump within the body drawing air through a port to create the grip vacuum, sensor monitoring that vacuum, indicator driven by the sensor, and battery powering the pump. The single relational limitation is the one the review confirmed as traceable: the indicator activates at a warning vacuum level greater than the release vacuum level at which the cup ceases to retain the load, which is the disclosure's "warns before a load can be dropped" expressed so that it has one meaning.

The dependent ladder now contains only limitations the ledger carries: activation before the load can be dropped, the release-level definition in the reviewer's own permitted wording, operation on the rechargeable battery without a cord to an external power supply (the review states that "cordless" is affirmative support for the absence of a cord alone), and the glass or stone panel as the load. Nothing was retained merely because it was a useful fallback.

The method claim was cut to the four steps that restate disclosed apparatus functions, in the terms the review permitted: placing the lip against the panel, drawing air through the port with the pump powered by the battery, monitoring the grip vacuum with the sensor, and activating the indicator at the warning vacuum level. The comparing decision, its loop, the maintaining step and the set-down step are gone, and with them claims that rested on them.

Numerals 64 and 66 were dropped rather than kept off-drawing. The graph sheet that displayed them is deleted as unsupported, and a numeral that appears in the text but on no drawing fails a mechanical check, so the warning vacuum level and the release vacuum level are now defined terms without numerals. That keeps the two permitted definitional sentences while leaving every numeral in the table on a sheet.

The figure plan was redistributed rather than pruned of disclosed parts. FIG. 1 carries the six structural numerals with no proportion, no coaxiality, no cup profile and no panel attitude; FIG. 2 carries the six functional numerals as plain rectangles and connections with no enclosure boundary, no unnumbered air lines, no flow arrows and no stated side of any axis; FIG. 3 carries the four step numerals as empty rectangles in one column. Six, six and four numerals per sheet.

The description paragraphs that introduce each figure now name only numerals that appear on that sheet, and the structural sentences about the pump being within the rigid body sit in a following paragraph that does not reference a figure, so no part is described as visible on a sheet that does not list it.

The near-vertical attitude sentence, the shear and tension and breakage assertions and the qualifier "planar" are removed, so the workpiece is simply a glass or stone panel, matching the disclosure and matching what FIG. 1 shows. The term "workpiece" was replaced by "panel" throughout for the same reason.

What remains of the technical argument is argument about the disclosed relationship, not added structure: why a threshold placed above the vacuum at which the cup lets go warns while the load is still held, and why a hand-carried tool needs that interval when a frame-mounted one does not. No apparatus, level, value or measurement supports it that the disclosure does not supply.

The Background retains its prior-art discussion, which the review placed outside its scope, but the two sentences that projected self-containment onto the invention were reduced to the hand-carried framing and the closing need statement now asks only for a cordless hand-held lifter that warns while the cup is still holding.

This summary introduces a selection of concepts that are described further in the detailed description. It is not intended to identify essential features of the claimed subject matter, nor to limit the scope of the claims.

A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is disclosed. The lifter has a rigid body comprising a handle, and a suction cup carried by the rigid body. The suction cup comprises a flexible sealing lip. An electric vacuum pump is disposed within the rigid body and draws air through a port to create a grip vacuum, the grip vacuum retaining a load on the suction cup. A pressure sensor monitors the grip vacuum. A warning indicator is driven by the pressure sensor. A rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump.

The grip vacuum is treated throughout this disclosure as a positive magnitude: it is the amount by which the pressure holding the suction cup to the load is below the ambient pressure outside the lifter, so that a larger grip vacuum means a firmer grip and a decaying grip is a falling grip vacuum.

The warning indicator activates when the grip vacuum falls to a warning vacuum level. The warning vacuum level is greater than a release vacuum level, the release vacuum level being the grip vacuum below which the suction cup can no longer retain the load. Because the warning vacuum level is greater than the release vacuum level, the grip vacuum on a decaying grip reaches the warning vacuum level first and the release vacuum level only afterwards. The warning indicator therefore activates while the suction cup is still retaining the load, that is, before the load can be dropped.

This ordering of levels is what makes the alarm useful in a hand-held tool rather than merely informative. A frame-mounted or suspended lifter can respond to a failing grip by itself, by cutting in a second vacuum source or by refusing to move. A cordless handheld lifter has no such recourse: the only actuator available is the person holding the handle, and a person needs an interval in which to act. Defining the warning threshold with respect to the release vacuum level is what makes that interval exist by construction rather than by luck.

Because the rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump, the lifter grips, monitors, and warns without a cord to an external power supply.

A method of lifting a glass or stone panel with such a lifter is also disclosed. The method includes placing the flexible sealing lip against the panel, drawing air through the port with the electric vacuum pump powered by the rechargeable battery to create the grip vacuum, lifting and carrying the panel by the handle, monitoring the grip vacuum with the pressure sensor while the panel is retained on the suction cup, and activating the warning indicator when the grip vacuum falls to the warning vacuum level, that is, while the suction cup still retains the panel and before the panel can be dropped.

A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to move glass panes, stone slabs, and similar flat panels on site by suction gripping. A suction cup is pressed against the face of the panel, air is removed from the space enclosed between the cup and the panel, and the resulting difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in that enclosed space clamps the cup to the panel so that the panel can be carried.

A suction grip is only as good as its seal. Dust on the panel, a textured or porous surface, a nick in the sealing lip, a change in temperature, or simply the slow permeation and leakage that occurs over minutes of handling will all bleed air back into the enclosed space. As air returns, the clamping force falls. The failure is progressive and, from the point of view of the person holding the panel, silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes until the cup lets go, at which point a heavy panel is already falling.

Vacuum lifting equipment has therefore long been fitted with vacuum monitoring. In one known lifter for transporting loads having an adhesion surface, a suction plate assembly carries projecting annular seals defining a vacuum chamber connected to a main vacuum source, a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that can be started by an emergency switch is additionally provided, and a pressure pickup associated with the vacuum chamber is coupled with a malfunction alarm such that the alarm is turned on when a preset limit pressure is exceeded during vacuum operation [REF:US-5310232-A]. That equipment is a suspended plate assembly with a main vacuum source and a separate emergency vacuum source; the alarm is described as a malfunction alarm tied to a preset limit pressure, and the reference does not describe the limit pressure in terms of the vacuum still needed to keep hold of the load.

Control systems for vacuum lift equipment have also been described in which a programmable controller interprets feedback from vacuum level sensors and battery sensors and responsively provides warnings and limits or alters machine functions, including evaluating a change in measured vacuum level over time to determine a rate of vacuum level change that may be caused by a leak and outputting a warning indication when that rate exceeds a threshold rate [REF:US-10518985-B2]. Such a system is built around a controller with memory, stored records, and machine-function interlocks, and its leak warning is a response to how fast the vacuum is changing rather than to where the vacuum sits relative to the point at which the grip would fail.

Powered suction devices in a hand-carried format are also known. An electric vacuum suction lifter has been described having a main body with a suction surface carrying first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space, a control unit, a vacuum pump controlled by the control unit to draw air from the sealed space, a pressure sensing unit that measures the pressure of the sealed space to generate instant pressure information, a battery unit that is charged by external power equipment and powers the control unit, pump, and pressure sensing unit, a start button, a pressure relief button, and at least one handle by which a member gripped by the device can be carried [REF:US-10625955-B2]. In that device the instant pressure information is compared with a high predetermined pressure and a low predetermined pressure: reaching the high predetermined pressure stops the pump, and falling below the low predetermined pressure restarts the pump. A warning unit is described as being operated when the detected battery power is below a predetermined battery power, and warning information relating to pressure is described as being transmitted to an external electronic device. A closely similar electric suction cup has likewise been described, in which the pressure detection unit detects the pressure between the suction cup and the component in real time and the vacuum pump automatically acts again when that pressure is lower than a second predetermined pressure [REF:CN-110630621-B].

Hand-carried suction devices that signal something about their own state are also known. A sucker for plate glass has been described having a sucker body defining a suction hole at a suction surface, a manually operatable vacuum pump carried on the body, a sensor communicating with the suction channel that connects the suction hole at the suction surface with the suction hole in the pump, and a sound generator that is turned on through a switch closed by the sensor when the degree of vacuum sensed reaches a predetermined value [REF:US-5184858-A]. The pump in that device is worked by hand rather than electrically, and the sound is generated at a predetermined degree of vacuum which the reference does not relate to the vacuum still needed to retain the sheet.

A portable hand grab has been described including one or more suction cups, at least one handle connected to the suction cups for gripping by hand, at least one electrical vacuum pump for at least partially evacuating the suction volume between the suction cups and the attachment surfaces, at least one vacuum sensor for detecting a vacuum level in the suction volume, and an electronic controller configured to control the pump to at least partially evacuate the suction volume when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being less than a preselected minimum vacuum level, optionally together with an attach indicator that the controller activates when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being greater than a preselected safe vacuum level [REF:WO-2017156581-A1]. The signal there tells the user that the vacuum is high enough to attach, and a vacuum below the preselected minimum vacuum level is answered by running the pump again rather than by telling the user that the grip is going.

A cordless wand device for grasping objects such as silicon wafers has been described having a housing with a hollow interior, a tip attached to the housing through a hollow tube and having a perimeter region contoured to form an airtight seal against the object, a power source and a vacuum pump positioned within the housing, and light-emitting diodes of different colours which indicate to an operator whether the power source is sufficiently charged to generate sufficient suction force to safely grasp the object, that sufficiency being determined from the voltage drop across resistors connected across the power source [REF:US-5374090-A]. What is indicated in that device is the state of the power source rather than the state of the grip on the object.

A portable electric carrying suction cup structure has been described in which a handle is fixed on the upper end of the suction cup body, a vacuum pump is provided on the suction cup body, and a control unit is connected between the power supply part and the vacuum pump, so that air continues to be pumped out after the suction cup body and the material surface have reached an airtight state; the control unit is provided with a pressure gauge by which the user can know the pressure change between the suction cup body and the surface, with a light source for displaying different usage states, and with a buzzer for sending out alarm sounds according to different usage states [REF:CN-2806399-Y]. That reference attributes the avoidance of loosening and falling during movement to the continued pumping, and it describes the buzzer as sounding according to different usage states without relating any sounding condition to the vacuum at which the cup would let go of the material.

A digital display suction cup has been described comprising a suction cup and a handle structure, the two ends of the handle structure being provided with a switch button and a pressure relief valve, the handle structure being provided with a battery and a vacuum electric pump which is connected to the suction cup through an air pipe, with an air pressure sensor and a display screen at the lower part of the battery end, a USB charging port electrically connected to the battery, and an inner side of the suction cup provided with an evacuation hole, a pressure relief hole, and a sensing through hole [REF:US-2024424646-A1]. That device monitors and maintains negative pressure in real time and shows the negative pressure value and the battery power on the display screen as numbers for the user to read.

Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1].

Three shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and the low pressure value at which it acts is chosen with reference to the working vacuum, not with reference to how much grip is left. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone. Second, where a signal is given, it is given on a condition unrelated to grip (battery state), on a rate of change, on a preset limit whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established, as a confirmation that the vacuum is high enough to attach, or as a number on a display which the user must look at and interpret while carrying a panel. None of these delivers the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.

Third, the equipment that has the most elaborate response to a failing grip is the equipment that is not carried in the hand. A suspended or frame-mounted assembly can cut in a second vacuum source or refuse further motion. A lifter that is carried in the hand has none of those remedies available to it: the only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle, and that person can only act if the notice arrives early enough.

There remains a need for a cordless, hand-held vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing while the cup is still holding, so that the warning arrives before the load can be dropped.

The grip vacuum is treated throughout this disclosure as a positive magnitude: it is the amount by which the pressure holding the suction cup to the load is below the ambient pressure outside the lifter, so that a larger grip vacuum means a firmer grip and a decaying grip is a falling grip vacuum.

The warning indicator activates when the grip vacuum is lost, and is configured to activate before the load can be dropped.

Because the rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump, the lifter grips, monitors, and warns without a cord to an external power supply.

A method of lifting a glass or stone panel with such a lifter is also disclosed. The method includes placing the flexible sealing lip against the panel, drawing air through the port with the electric vacuum pump powered by the rechargeable battery to create the grip vacuum, lifting and carrying the panel by the handle, monitoring the grip vacuum with the pressure sensor while the panel is retained on the suction cup, and activating the warning indicator upon loss of the grip vacuum, before the panel can be dropped.

In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

Terminology used in this disclosure has the following meanings. The grip vacuum is the vacuum created when an electric vacuum pump 20 of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter draws air through a port 22, expressed as a positive magnitude: it is the amount by which the pressure holding the suction cup 10 to the load is below the ambient atmospheric pressure surrounding the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. A grip vacuum of zero corresponds to no grip at all; the grip vacuum rises as the electric vacuum pump 20 draws air away and falls as the grip decays. Statements that the grip vacuum is greater or higher therefore mean that the grip is firmer. This convention is used consistently in the description, in the drawings, and in the claims.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. In use, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a panel 50 of glass or stone, and the panel 50 is the load which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 carries.

FIG. 2 shows schematically the suction cup 10, the port 22, the electric vacuum pump 20, a pressure sensor 30, a warning indicator 32, and a rechargeable battery 40, and the connections among them.

The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14 and is configured to draw air through the port 22 to create a grip vacuum, by which grip vacuum the suction cup 10 retains the load. The pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the grip vacuum. The warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. The rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20.

The warning indicator 32 activates when the grip vacuum is lost, and is configured to activate before the load can be dropped.

The rechargeable battery 40 is the power supply for the electric vacuum pump 20, so that the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 grips, monitors the grip vacuum, and warns without a cord to an external power supply, including while the panel 50 is carried.

The panel 50 is a glass or stone panel, and the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the panel 50 when the panel 50 is to be lifted.

FIG. 3 is a flow diagram of a method of lifting a panel with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter, the method comprising a placing step 202, an evacuating step 204, a monitoring step 206, and an activating step 208.

At the placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the panel 50. At the evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the grip vacuum, and the panel 50 is lifted and carried by the handle 16, the panel 50 being retained on the suction cup 10 by the grip vacuum. At the monitoring step 206, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the panel 50 is retained on the suction cup 10. At the activating step 208, upon loss of the grip vacuum, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate. The activating step 208 occurs before the panel 50 can be dropped.

The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.

tool_use_result.originalFile:
A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to move glass panes, stone slabs, and similar flat panels on site by suction gripping. A suction cup is pressed against the face of the panel, air is removed from the space enclosed between the cup and the panel, and the resulting difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in that enclosed space clamps the cup to the panel so that the panel can be carried.

A suction grip is only as good as its seal. Dust on the panel, a textured or porous surface, a nick in the sealing lip, a change in temperature, or simply the slow permeation and leakage that occurs over minutes of handling will all bleed air back into the enclosed space. As air returns, the clamping force falls. The failure is progressive and, from the point of view of the person holding the panel, silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes until the cup lets go, at which point a heavy panel is already falling.

Vacuum lifting equipment has therefore long been fitted with vacuum monitoring. In one known lifter for transporting loads having an adhesion surface, a suction plate assembly carries projecting annular seals defining a vacuum chamber connected to a main vacuum source, a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that can be started by an emergency switch is additionally provided, and a pressure pickup associated with the vacuum chamber is coupled with a malfunction alarm such that the alarm is turned on when a preset limit pressure is exceeded during vacuum operation [REF:US-5310232-A]. That equipment is a suspended plate assembly with a main vacuum source and a separate emergency vacuum source; the alarm is described as a malfunction alarm tied to a preset limit pressure, and the reference does not describe the limit pressure in terms of the vacuum still needed to keep hold of the load.

Control systems for vacuum lift equipment have also been described in which a programmable controller interprets feedback from vacuum level sensors and battery sensors and responsively provides warnings and limits or alters machine functions, including evaluating a change in measured vacuum level over time to determine a rate of vacuum level change that may be caused by a leak and outputting a warning indication when that rate exceeds a threshold rate [REF:US-10518985-B2]. Such a system is built around a controller with memory, stored records, and machine-function interlocks, and its leak warning is a response to how fast the vacuum is changing rather than to where the vacuum sits relative to the point at which the grip would fail.

Powered suction devices in a hand-carried format are also known. An electric vacuum suction lifter has been described having a main body with a suction surface carrying first and second annular sealing units that bound a sealed space, a control unit, a vacuum pump controlled by the control unit to draw air from the sealed space, a pressure sensing unit that measures the pressure of the sealed space to generate instant pressure information, a battery unit that is charged by external power equipment and powers the control unit, pump, and pressure sensing unit, a start button, a pressure relief button, and at least one handle by which a member gripped by the device can be carried [REF:US-10625955-B2]. In that device the instant pressure information is compared with a high predetermined pressure and a low predetermined pressure: reaching the high predetermined pressure stops the pump, and falling below the low predetermined pressure restarts the pump. A warning unit is described as being operated when the detected battery power is below a predetermined battery power, and warning information relating to pressure is described as being transmitted to an external electronic device. A closely similar electric suction cup has likewise been described, in which the pressure detection unit detects the pressure between the suction cup and the component in real time and the vacuum pump automatically acts again when that pressure is lower than a second predetermined pressure [REF:CN-110630621-B].

Hand-carried suction devices that signal something about their own state are also known. A sucker for plate glass has been described having a sucker body defining a suction hole at a suction surface, a manually operatable vacuum pump carried on the body, a sensor communicating with the suction channel that connects the suction hole at the suction surface with the suction hole in the pump, and a sound generator that is turned on through a switch closed by the sensor when the degree of vacuum sensed reaches a predetermined value [REF:US-5184858-A]. The pump in that device is worked by hand rather than electrically, and the sound is generated at a predetermined degree of vacuum which the reference does not relate to the vacuum still needed to retain the sheet.

A portable hand grab has been described including one or more suction cups, at least one handle connected to the suction cups for gripping by hand, at least one electrical vacuum pump for at least partially evacuating the suction volume between the suction cups and the attachment surfaces, at least one vacuum sensor for detecting a vacuum level in the suction volume, and an electronic controller configured to control the pump to at least partially evacuate the suction volume when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being less than a preselected minimum vacuum level, optionally together with an attach indicator that the controller activates when the vacuum sensor detects the vacuum level being greater than a preselected safe vacuum level [REF:WO-2017156581-A1]. The signal there tells the user that the vacuum is high enough to attach, and a vacuum below the preselected minimum vacuum level is answered by running the pump again rather than by telling the user that the grip is going.

A cordless wand device for grasping objects such as silicon wafers has been described having a housing with a hollow interior, a tip attached to the housing through a hollow tube and having a perimeter region contoured to form an airtight seal against the object, a power source and a vacuum pump positioned within the housing, and light-emitting diodes of different colours which indicate to an operator whether the power source is sufficiently charged to generate sufficient suction force to safely grasp the object, that sufficiency being determined from the voltage drop across resistors connected across the power source [REF:US-5374090-A]. What is indicated in that device is the state of the power source rather than the state of the grip on the object.

A portable electric carrying suction cup structure has been described in which a handle is fixed on the upper end of the suction cup body, a vacuum pump is provided on the suction cup body, and a control unit is connected between the power supply part and the vacuum pump, so that air continues to be pumped out after the suction cup body and the material surface have reached an airtight state; the control unit is provided with a pressure gauge by which the user can know the pressure change between the suction cup body and the surface, with a light source for displaying different usage states, and with a buzzer for sending out alarm sounds according to different usage states [REF:CN-2806399-Y]. That reference attributes the avoidance of loosening and falling during movement to the continued pumping, and it describes the buzzer as sounding according to different usage states without relating any sounding condition to the vacuum at which the cup would let go of the material.

A digital display suction cup has been described comprising a suction cup and a handle structure, the two ends of the handle structure being provided with a switch button and a pressure relief valve, the handle structure being provided with a battery and a vacuum electric pump which is connected to the suction cup through an air pipe, with an air pressure sensor and a display screen at the lower part of the battery end, a USB charging port electrically connected to the battery, and an inner side of the suction cup provided with an evacuation hole, a pressure relief hole, and a sensing through hole [REF:US-2024424646-A1]. That device monitors and maintains negative pressure in real time and shows the negative pressure value and the battery power on the display screen as numbers for the user to read.

Multi-cup handling equipment has been described in which two or more vacuum modules are mounted on a mounting frame, each module having a cup, an electrically powered vacuum pump, a fluid circuit, a controller, and optionally a pressure sensor and a battery, with an interface through which a user selects an operational mode of the modules, and in which each module may include indicators that indicate a functional condition of the module visually or audibly [REF:WO-2022236379-A1].

Three shortcomings persist for a person who is holding a panel in one hand. First, the response to a decaying grip in the known powered devices is to run the pump again: the device treats a falling vacuum as a housekeeping event to be corrected, and the low pressure value at which it acts is chosen with reference to the working vacuum, not with reference to how much grip is left. If the leak is larger than the pump can make up - a torn lip, a dusty or porous panel, a cracked substrate - the pump simply runs while the grip continues to decay, and the user is told nothing until the panel is gone. Second, where a signal is given, it is given on a condition unrelated to grip (battery state), on a rate of change, on a preset limit whose relationship to the load-holding capacity of the cup is not established, as a confirmation that the vacuum is high enough to attach, or as a number on a display which the user must look at and interpret while carrying a panel. None of these delivers the one thing a person carrying a slab actually needs: notice that arrives while the cup is still holding, with grip left over to get the panel down.

Third, the equipment that has the most elaborate response to a failing grip is the equipment that is not carried in the hand. A suspended plate assembly can be provided with a battery-fed emergency vacuum source that an emergency switch starts [REF:US-5310232-A], and a controller for vacuum lift equipment can limit or alter machine functions in response to sensor feedback [REF:US-10518985-B2]. A lifter that is carried in the hand has none of those remedies available to it: the only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle, and that person can only act if the notice arrives early enough.

There remains a need for a cordless, hand-held vacuum lifter that tells the user that the grip is failing while the cup is still holding, so that the warning arrives before the load can be dropped.

input.summary: Applied the four fixes the review called for, each self-contained and adding nothing beyond the disclosure. The terminology paragraph no longer claims the positive-magnitude convention is carried through the drawings, so the Detailed Description and the Brief Description of the Drawings now agree. The Background's closing need statement uses "handheld", matching the title, claims, abstract, numeral table and figure briefs. The evacuating step 204 covers only the drawing of air that creates the grip vacuum; lifting and carrying the panel by the handle is now a separate sentence outside the numbered step, so 204 means one thing in the numeral table, the FIG. 3 brief and the description, and the flow diagram no longer absorbs a separately claimed act. The claimed relationship that the electric vacuum pump is disposed within the rigid body is now illustrated: FIG. 1's brief adds the pump in broken lines within the outline of the rigid body with its position expressly insignificant and no other internal part drawn, numeral 20 is added to that brief's table and shown-numerals list, the Brief Description of FIG. 1 says so, and the FIG. 1 paragraph of the description points to it. FIG. 1 now carries seven numerals, the numeral table is unchanged at 15 entries, and every numeral remains used in the text and shown on a sheet.
reasoning: The grip-vacuum convention sentence was narrowed to the description and the claims rather than curing the mismatch with a new drawing, because no inventor passage discloses any vacuum level or magnitude that a drawing could depict; the only source text is that the sensor monitors the grip vacuum and the indicator activates when vacuum is lost.

Splitting the evacuating step sentence keeps the lifting and carrying in the description, where it is supported as the function of handle 16 on a lifter for panels and where method claim 5 recites it as its own step, while detaching it from numbered step 204. That preserves both the claim step and the four-box flow diagram without touching numerals.md or the FIG. 3 brief.

For the pump-within-the-body relationship the invention text was left as it stands and the drawing was brought up to it: the pump is drawn in broken lines inside the rigid body outline, which depicts exactly the inventor's statement that the pump is disposed inside the body. The brief states that its position within the outline is not significant and that no other internal part is drawn, so the sheet adds no layout, proportion, connection or internal structure to the disclosure.

Numeral 20 now appears on FIG. 1 as well as FIG. 2, and FIG. 1 rises from six to seven numerals, within the per-sheet limit. The description paragraph that introduces FIG. 1 names only numerals listed on that sheet, and the same holds for the FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 paragraphs.

This summary introduces a selection of concepts that are described further in the detailed description. It is not intended to identify essential features of the claimed subject matter, nor to limit the scope of the claims.

A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is disclosed. The lifter has a rigid body comprising a handle, and a suction cup carried by the rigid body. The suction cup comprises a flexible sealing lip. An electric vacuum pump is disposed within the rigid body and draws air through a port to create a grip vacuum, the grip vacuum retaining a load on the suction cup. A pressure sensor monitors the grip vacuum. A warning indicator is driven by the pressure sensor. A rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump.

The grip vacuum is treated throughout this disclosure as a positive magnitude: it is the amount by which the pressure holding the suction cup to the load is below the ambient pressure outside the lifter, so that a larger grip vacuum means a firmer grip and a decaying grip is a falling grip vacuum.

The warning indicator activates when the grip vacuum is lost, and is configured to activate before the load can be dropped.

Because the rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump, the lifter grips, monitors, and warns without a cord to an external power supply.

A method of lifting a glass or stone panel with such a lifter is also disclosed. The method includes placing the flexible sealing lip against the panel, drawing air through the port with the electric vacuum pump powered by the rechargeable battery to create the grip vacuum, lifting and carrying the panel by the handle, monitoring the grip vacuum with the pressure sensor while the panel is retained on the suction cup, and activating the warning indicator upon loss of the grip vacuum, before the panel can be dropped.

In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

Terminology used in this disclosure has the following meanings. The grip vacuum is the vacuum created when an electric vacuum pump 20 of the cordless handheld vacuum lifter draws air through a port 22, expressed as a positive magnitude: it is the amount by which the pressure between the suction cup 10 and the load is below the ambient atmospheric pressure surrounding the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. A grip vacuum of zero corresponds to no grip at all; the grip vacuum rises as the electric vacuum pump 20 draws air away and falls as the grip decays. Statements that the grip vacuum is greater or higher therefore mean that the grip is firmer. This convention is used consistently in the description and in the claims.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. In use, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a panel 50 of glass or stone, and the panel 50 is the load which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 carries. The electric vacuum pump 20, being disposed within the rigid body 14, is shown in broken lines in FIG. 1.

FIG. 2 shows schematically the suction cup 10, the port 22, the electric vacuum pump 20, a pressure sensor 30, a warning indicator 32, and a rechargeable battery 40, and the connections among them.

The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14 and is configured to draw air through the port 22 to create a grip vacuum, by which grip vacuum the suction cup 10 retains the load. The pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the grip vacuum. The warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. The rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20.

The warning indicator 32 activates when the grip vacuum is lost, and is configured to activate before the load can be dropped.

The rechargeable battery 40 powers the electric vacuum pump 20, so that the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 grips, monitors the grip vacuum, and warns without a cord to an external power supply, including while the panel 50 is carried.

The panel 50 is a glass or stone panel, and the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the panel 50 when the panel 50 is to be lifted.

FIG. 3 is a flow diagram of a method of lifting a panel with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter, the method comprising a placing step 202, an evacuating step 204, a monitoring step 206, and an activating step 208.

At the placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the panel 50. At the evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the grip vacuum. The panel 50 is then lifted and carried by the handle 16, the panel 50 being retained on the suction cup 10 by the grip vacuum. At the monitoring step 206, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the grip vacuum while the panel 50 is retained on the suction cup 10. At the activating step 208, upon loss of the grip vacuum, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate. The activating step 208 occurs before the panel 50 can be dropped.

The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.
